_readme: OREGON CIVIL DEADLINE RULES -- 6 rows, ORCP 7 C(2), 43 B(2) and 45 B.
== THERE IS NO INTERROGATORY ROW, AND THAT IS THE LAW =================
READ THIS FIRST, because an absent row otherwise looks like unfinished
work. OREGON HAS NO WRITTEN INTERROGATORIES IN CIVIL DISCOVERY AT ALL.
Searching the entire ORCP for `interrogator` returns FOUR hits and all
four are JURY interrogatories under Rule 61 C (a general verdict
accompanied by answers to interrogatories). There is no
discovery-interrogatory rule to seed.
Every other seeded jurisdiction has an interrogatory row. Oregon must
have none. Do not go looking for one and do not add it by analogy to
Nevada's NRCP 33 or Utah's URCP 33.
== SOURCE: TAKE THE TEXT FROM THE LEGISLATURE, NOT THE COUNCIL ========
Oregon's civil rules are NOT promulgated by the Supreme Court. The
COUNCIL ON COURT PROCEDURES, a statutory public body, drafts and
promulgates the ORCP; the Legislative Assembly may then amend or repeal
them, and they take effect as law the following 1 January. That
two-stage lifecycle is visible in the rules' own citation lines, which
carry TWO amending authorities -- `CCP 12/6/14` alongside `2015 c.212
s.8`. No other seeded jurisdiction has this.
AND THE COUNCIL'S OWN SITE SAYS ITS COPY IS NOT AUTHORITATIVE: `the
first link is static and may not include the most recent Council
amendments nor amendments by the Legislature`. Its static copy is
labelled `ORCP - Effective January 1, 2020` while its own news page
records 2024 promulgations that copy does not reflect.
SO THE TEXT HERE COMES FROM THE LEGISLATURE'S FILE:
oregonlegislature.gov/bills_laws/SiteAssets/ORCP.html -- HTTP 200 on a
BARE curl, ~1.1 MB, one HTML file of the whole ORCP, headed `Oregon
Rules of Civil Procedure (2025)`. ORS 187 and ORS 174 come from the
same host, the same way.
STANDING TWO-CHANNEL RULE FOR ANY OREGON RE-READ: the Legislature's file
is the TEXT; the Council's promulgation record is the FORWARD channel,
showing what becomes law next 1 January before the Legislature's copy
reflects it. Check both, in that order. Same shape as Maryland's Rules
Orders, arrived at for a completely different structural reason.
== THE WEEKEND QUESTION -- SAFE, AND THE DRAFTING IS WHY ==============
ORCP 10 A rolls off `a Saturday or a legal holiday, INCLUDING SUNDAY`.
Saturday is named SEPARATELY and Sunday is folded INTO the holiday
definition. So even though ORS 187.010(1)(a) makes `Each Sunday` a legal
holiday -- the same statutory quirk that BLOCKED Louisiana -- Oregon's
rule rolls off Saturday in its own right, statewide. isWeekend() is
correct here because of how the PROCEDURAL RULE is drafted, not because
of the holiday statute. The two states' statutes look alike; the rules
do not.
== ORCP 10 A ANSWERS A QUESTION MARYLAND LEAVES OPEN ==================
The threshold is measured on the period `(WITHOUT REGARD TO SECTION B OF
THIS RULE)` -- section B being the service extension. So the 7-day test
runs on the BASE period, BEFORE the three days are added.
Maryland logged the identical question as an open decision with no
authority found either way. Oregon does not decide Maryland, but it
shows the question is a known one and which way one drafter resolved it.
This engine already behaves Oregon's way -- the exclusion is applied
during base-period counting, before any extension -- and
deadline-oregon.test.js ASSERTS it rather than assuming it, so a future
change made for Maryland cannot silently break Oregon.
== WHICH ROWS CARRY THE EXTENSION -- STATED BY THE RULE, NOT INFERRED ==
ORCP 10 B opens `EXCEPT FOR SERVICE OF SUMMONS`. Four words at the front
of the sentence doing what every other jurisdiction made this project
INFER from which rule authorises the service -- an inference that had
been got WRONG on two federal rows (corrected 2026-08-27) and that
Arkansas states in a proviso at the back.
So the two ORCP 7 C(2) rows carry NO service_extension and the four
discovery rows do. Nothing here rests on inference.
ALL FOUR METHODS QUALIFY: mail, e-mail, facsimile communication and
electronic service, all +3. That is the OPPOSITE of Nevada, West
Virginia, New York and the federal rule, where e-service takes nothing.
An allowlist copied from the federal family would UNDER-count and
compute EARLY. `Added to the prescribed period` -> period-lengthening,
not the federal after-expiry order.
== THE DISCOVERY FLOORS ARE resolve_periods, NOT A SHARED COUNT =======
Both discovery rules give a defendant the LATER of the ordinary 30 days
and 45 days from service of the summons. DIFFERENT COUNTS PER LIMB, so
this is `resolve_periods: later_of` -- the shape built after Georgia's
O.C.G.A. 9-11-36(a)(2) shipped FIFTEEN DAYS EARLY -- and not the plain
`resolve: later_of` that Nevada's government row uses, where both limbs
share one count.
BOTH LIMBS RUN FROM CALLER-SUPPLIED DATES, so Oregon does NOT hit the
Maryland chained-floor gap where one limb depends on another rule's
computed output. The engine REFUSES unless both dates are supplied.
AND THE TWO FLOORS DO NOT SHARE A TRIGGER. Rule 43 B(2)'s second limb
runs from service of the SUMMONS; Rule 45 B's runs from service of the
SUMMONS AND COMPLAINT. The trigger names differ deliberately and are NOT
interchangeable -- they are separate events in ORCP 7 and a caller who
supplies one for the other is answering a different question.
== WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT SEEDED ===================================
(1) Any interrogatory row -- see the top of this readme.
(2) Any BACKWARD row. ORCP 10 A contains no backward provision at all,
so or_orcp_10's rollover_suffix_backward is BLANK -- the
NJ/NC/WA/MA/MO/WI position, not Minnesota's, Utah's or Nevada's.
(3) Any row whose period is fixed by STATUTE rather than by the ORCP.
ORCP 10 A ends `This section does not apply to any time limitation
governed by ORS 174.120`, and 174.120 is the statutory computation
rule. It counts the same way -- exclude the first day, include the
last unless it is `a legal holiday or Saturday`, roll to the next day
the court is open -- but it has NO SHORT-PERIOD EXCLUSION AT ALL.
A statutory Oregon period computed under or_orcp_10 would wrongly
drop intermediate days on any period under 7. Every row here takes
its period from the ORCP, so the carve-out is not reached; a
statutory row would need its own standard.
(4) Appellate rows -- the ORAP are a separate body of rules.
== NOT MODELLED, ALL EARLY, DISCLOSED ================================
ORCP 10 A's public-office-closure limb is the BROADEST encountered: it
fires when the office is closed `before the end of OR FOR ALL OF the
normal work day`, so a PARTIAL-day closure counts, and the period then
runs `until the close of office hours on the next day the office is
open`. It is ADDITIONAL to the Saturday/holiday rollover rather than a
replacement, so omitting it can only report EARLY.
ORS 187.020(1) gubernatorial appointments are ad hoc. ORS 187.020(2) is
CONJUNCTIVE and worth stating because the obvious assumption runs the
other way: a day appointed by the PRESIDENT is an Oregon legal holiday
ONLY IF the Governor also appoints it. A presidential day alone is not.
Both discovery rules carry court-order escapes the engine cannot see --
`or such other time as the court may order`, `unless the court specifies
a shorter time`, `within such shorter or longer time as the court may
allow`.
ORCP 7 D (manner of service) was not read, so what date a caller should
supply as `the date of service` is not sourced from the rule text. The
publication row is safer in this respect: the rule states outright that
the date in the summons IS the date of first publication.

rules.label: Appear and defend after service of the summons (Oregon) — NOT styled as an answer

authority.quote: If the summons is served by any manner other than publication, the defendant shall appear and defend within 30 days from the date of service.
authority.note: THIRTY DAYS, AND THE OBLIGATION IS TO 'APPEAR AND DEFEND', NOT TO FILE AN ANSWER. The rule's own notice to defendants explains what that means in practice — 'To "appear" you must file with the court a legal document called a "motion" or "answer"' — so either satisfies it, and this must not be read as an answer-only deadline. NO SERVICE EXTENSION, AND THAT IS THE RULE'S OWN WORDS RATHER THAN AN INFERENCE: ORCP 10 B opens 'Except for service of summons'. Every other jurisdiction made this project infer the Rule 4 / Rule 5 scope split from which rule authorises the service — an inference got wrong on two federal rows and corrected 2026-08-27. Oregon states it in four words at the front of the sentence. The publication limb is a SEPARATE ROW because it runs from a different date. ORCP 7 D (manner of service) was not read, so what a caller should supply as 'the date of service' is not sourced here.

rules.label: Appear and defend after service by publication (Oregon)

authority.quote: If the summons is served by publication pursuant to subparagraph D(6)(a)(i) of this rule, the defendant shall appear and defend within 30 days from the date stated in the summons. The date so stated in the summons shall be the date of the first publication.
authority.note: THIRTY DAYS, SAME COUNT AS THE ORDINARY ROW, DIFFERENT TRIGGER — which is exactly why it is its own row rather than a note on the other. The rule then does something unusually helpful: it says outright that the date stated in the summons IS the date of first publication, so the caller has one unambiguous date to supply. Contrast the ordinary row, where 'the date of service' depends on ORCP 7 D, which was not read. NO SERVICE EXTENSION: ORCP 10 B's 'Except for service of summons' reaches this limb too.

rules.label: Response to a request to produce or inspect (Oregon)

authority.quote: Otherwise, within 30 days after service of a request in accordance with subsection B(1) of this rule, or such other time as the court may order or to which th
authority.note: THIRTY DAYS FOR A PARTY WHO IS NOT A DEFENDANT, or for a defendant whose 45-day floor has already passed. A DEFENDANT SHOULD USE THE later-of ROW INSTEAD — relying on this one alone can produce a date up to 45 days too early. The quote is truncated at the boundary of what was read and is marked as such rather than completed from memory; the operative period and trigger are verbatim, and the sentence continues into court-order and party-agreement escapes the engine cannot see. NOTE THE FLOOR IS PHRASED AS A LIMIT ON WHAT THE REQUEST MAY DEMAND — 'A request may not require a defendant to produce ... before the expiration of 45 days after service of summons' — not as a period the responding party is given. The practical effect is the same and the later-of row models it, but the wording differs from Rule 45 B's and the two should not be normalised to each other.

service_extension.note: ORCP 10 B: three days for mail, e-mail, facsimile communication OR electronic service — the broadest enumeration in the platform, and the opposite of Nevada, West Virginia, New York and the federal rule, where e-service takes nothing. DO NOT NARROW THIS ALLOWLIST by analogy to them. 'Added to the prescribed period' means the days lengthen the period and one rollover runs at the end, not the federal after-expiry order.

rules.label: Response to a request to produce — DEFENDANT, the later of 30 days and the 45-day floor (Oregon)

limbs.label: 30 days after service of the request
45 days after service of the summons

authority.quote: A request may not require a defendant to produce or allow inspection, copying, entry, or other related acts before the expiration of 45 days after service of summons, unless the court specifies a shorter time.
authority.note: TWO LIMBS WITH DIFFERENT COUNTS — 30 from the request, 45 from the summons — so this is resolve_periods and NOT the plain resolve: later_of that Nevada's government row uses, where both limbs share one count. That distinction is the reason resolve_periods exists: Georgia's O.C.G.A. 9-11-36(a)(2) was first encoded as an ordinary later_of and shipped FIFTEEN DAYS EARLY, because later_of picks the later trigger DATE and then applies one count. THE ENGINE REFUSES UNLESS BOTH DATES ARE SUPPLIED, because resolving from one limb would be too early whenever the other governs. BOTH LIMBS RUN FROM CALLER-SUPPLIED DATES, so Oregon does not hit the Maryland chained-floor gap. THIS LIMB RUNS FROM THE SUMMONS ALONE; Rule 45 B's runs from the SUMMONS AND COMPLAINT, and the trigger names differ deliberately — they are not interchangeable. 'Unless the court specifies a shorter time' is an order the engine cannot see. NO SERVICE EXTENSION ON THIS ROW: no seeded rule combines resolve_periods with an extension, the engine has never been exercised on that combination, and inventing the interaction — does the extension lengthen one limb or both, before or after the later-of resolves — would be guessing at an order no rule text settles. Compute the plain row for the extension and compare.

rules.label: Response to requests for admission (Oregon) — SILENCE ADMITS

authority.quote: The matter is admitted unless, within 30 days after service of the request, or within such shorter or longer time as the court may allow, the party to whom the request is directed serves on the party requesting the admission a written answer or objection addressed to the matter, signed by the party or by the party's attorney; but, unless the court shortens the time, a defendant shall not be required to serve answers or objections before the expiration of 45 days after service of the summons and complaint on that defendant.
authority.note: THIRTY DAYS, AND MISSING IT ADMITS THE MATTER — the rule is phrased as 'the matter is admitted unless', not as a duty to respond. OREGON GOES FURTHER THAN MOST AND REQUIRES THE WARNING ON THE FACE OF THE REQUEST: Rule 45 A obliges the requesting party to print, in capitals, 'FAILURE TO SERVE A WRITTEN ANSWER OR OBJECTION WITHIN THE TIME ALLOWED BY ORCP 45 B WILL RESULT IN ADMISSION OF THE FOLLOWING REQUESTS.' The same mandatory-warning device Missouri's R. 59.01(a)(1) has, and unlike Nevada, which requires no warning at all. THIS ROW IS FOR A PARTY WHO IS NOT A DEFENDANT, or a defendant whose 45-day floor has passed; a defendant should use the later-of row, since relying on this one alone can produce a date up to 45 days too early — and here that does not merely mislead, it can concede the matter.

service_extension.note: See the production row. All four methods qualify — mail, e-mail, facsimile and electronic service — and the allowlist must not be narrowed by analogy to the federal family.

rules.label: Response to requests for admission — DEFENDANT, the later of 30 days and the 45-day floor (Oregon)

limbs.label: 30 days after service of the request
45 days after service of the summons and complaint

authority.quote: but, unless the court shortens the time, a defendant shall not be required to serve answers or objections before the expiration of 45 days after service of the summons and complaint on that defendant.
authority.note: FORTY-FIVE DAYS ON THE SECOND LIMB, and the consequence of getting it wrong is worse here than on the production row: silence ADMITS under Rule 45 B, so a date computed 45 days early does not merely mislead — it can cost the matter. THIS LIMB RUNS FROM SERVICE OF THE SUMMONS AND COMPLAINT, where Rule 43 B(2)'s runs from service of the SUMMONS ALONE. The trigger names differ deliberately and are NOT interchangeable. THE ENGINE REFUSES UNLESS BOTH DATES ARE SUPPLIED. NO SERVICE EXTENSION ON THIS ROW, for the same reason as the production later-of row: no seeded rule combines resolve_periods with an extension and the interaction is not settled by any rule text.
